strengths: Principled and well-motivated approach: The paper addresses a well-known bottleneck in Neural CDEs—namely, that exact spline interpolants transmit raw signal noise into high-order path derivatives, which causes adaptive ODE solvers to take excessively small steps and inflates the Number of Function Evaluations (NFE).

Sound theoretical analysis: Theorems 3.1–3.4 establish clear connections between path smoothness/regularity, kernel bandwidth $h$, and adaptive solver step size, showing that smoothing priors decouple NFE from noise amplitude and characterizing the bottleneck behavior of parallel integration.

Effective combination of smoothing with multi-view attention: The proposed MV-CDE and MVC-CDE architectures provide a natural mechanism to recover high-frequency information lost during smoothing by using learnable queries and local 1D convolutions across multi-scale paths.

Comprehensive empirical speed and robustness evaluation: On the evaluated benchmarks, MVC-CDE (GP) demonstrates significant reductions in NFE and total wall-clock training time compared to standard linear/cubic CDEs, along with substantially higher robustness to additive Gaussian noise.
weaknesses: Unclear training mechanics and computational cost of the weighted GP formulation: Section 3.5 introduces learnable queries $Q$ and a CNN $\Phi_{\text{conv}}$ to compute observation-wise attention weights $\alpha_{m,k}$, which determine the diagonal noise covariance matrix $\Sigma_m$. However, Section 3.4 and Appendix C.4 state that GP path fitting is a 'static, one-time preprocessing cost' (shown as minimal overhead in Figure 10). If the attention weights depend on trainable parameters ($Q$ and $\Phi_{\text{conv}}$), $(K_h + \Sigma_m)^{-1}$ must either be re-inverted and differentiated through during training iterations, or the weights must be decoupled from end-to-end training. The manuscript does not sufficiently clarify whether and how gradients backpropagate through the GP inversion during training.

Evaluation restricted to regularly sampled datasets: A primary motivation for Neural CDEs is modeling irregularly sampled and asynchronous time series with missing observations. However, all three experimental benchmarks (CharacterTrajectories, SpokenArabicDigits, UWaveGestureLibrary) are regularly sampled time series with uniform $\Delta t = 1$ and rectilinear padding. Evaluating on standard irregular time series benchmarks (e.g., PhysioNet Challenge 2012 / 2019) is necessary to demonstrate that attentive smoothing retains its efficiency and modeling advantages under genuine irregularity and missingness.

Presentation and layout of main experimental results: The primary quantitative results table (Table 1) is referenced in the main body (Section 4.1) but only appears in the Appendix on page 18. The main text relies solely on small-scale scatter plots (Figure 3), which diminishes the clarity and self-containment of the main manuscript.

Missing comparisons with recent efficient continuous-depth baselines: While the paper compares against standard Neural CDEs and Log-NCDE, other recent methods targeting efficient ODE/CDE execution (such as Structured Linear CDEs or seminorm-based adjoint solvers) are discussed in related work but omitted from the empirical benchmarks.

strengths: Principled problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes a major computational bottleneck in Neural CDEs—namely, that exact spline interpolation preserves noise and high-frequency variations, which inflates the higher-order derivatives of the driving path and causes adaptive ODE solvers to take excessively small steps.

Solid theoretical motivation: The connection between the (p+1)-th derivative of the control path, the local truncation error of Runge-Kutta solvers (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2), and the parallel integration bottleneck (Theorem 3.4) provides good mathematical backing for why kernel/GP smoothing controls solver stiffness.

Multi-view attentive architecture: Mitigating over-smoothing via multiple smoothed views modulated by attention weights (and heteroscedastic noise covariance in GPs) is an innovative architectural concept.
Comprehensive empirical analysis: The manuscript includes detailed Pareto efficiency curves, NFE measurements, noise perturbation experiments, head-count ablations, and runtime breakdowns.
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity regarding end-to-end training vs. precomputation: In Section 3.4 and Appendix C.4, the authors state that GP matrix inversion is a 'static, one-time preprocessing cost' that incurs minimal overhead. However, in Section 3.5 (Eq. 4), the GP path $X^{(m)}(t) = k_h(t)^\top (K_h + \Sigma_m)^{-1} X$ explicitly relies on head-specific noise covariance $\Sigma_m$, which is parameterized by attention scores $\alpha_{m,k}$ computed from learnable queries $Q$ and conv network $\Phi_{conv}$. If $Q$ and $\Phi_{conv}$ are trained end-to-end via gradient descent, the $N \times N$ matrix inversion $(K_h + \Sigma_m)^{-1}$ must be recomputed and backpropagated through at every training step for every sample and head, which contradicts the claim that it is a static, one-time precomputation. If it is precomputed, the paper fails to explain how $\alpha_{m,k}$ can be learned dynamically.

Evaluation on regularized/padded grids rather than true irregular benchmarks: A core raison d'être of Neural CDEs is their continuous-time handling of irregularly sampled, asynchronous data with missing values. However, Section B.2 specifies that the data is padded to maximum sequence length using rectilinear padding with uniform time steps $\Delta t = 1$. The paper does not evaluate on standard irregularly sampled benchmarks (e.g., PhysioNet 2012, MIMIC-III, or irregular MuJoCo/climate time series), leaving the effectiveness of the method on genuinely irregular time series unverified.

Scaling to longer sequence lengths: Exact GP smoothing scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ per sample, and evaluating $M$ parallel continuous paths scales integration and state memory proportionally. While the sequence lengths evaluated are relatively short ($N \le 315$), this setup does not appear scalable to long-horizon time series without state-space or sparse GP approximations, which are not explored.

Missing comparisons with discrete architectures designed for regular series: Since the evaluation is restricted to regularly spaced time series with $\Delta t = 1$, standard discrete sequence models (1D ResNets, ConvNets, Transformers, or S4/Mamba) provide natural points of comparison. In Table 1, GRU-D already trains in 2–10 seconds and is competitive with or superior to many CDE configurations, questioning the necessity of a continuous-time differential equation when the underlying time grid is regular.

strengths: The core insight that numerical stiffness in Neural CDEs is largely driven by exact interpolation of noisy data, rather than purely the latent vector field, is well-motivated and addresses an important practical bottleneck of continuous-time sequence models.

The proposed smoothing approach successfully demonstrates significant empirical reductions in ODE solver evaluations (NFE) and exhibits improved stability under additive white Gaussian noise compared to standard spline interpolants (as illustrated in Figure 4).

The empirical analysis provides interesting ablation studies and visualizations, including attention map visualizations (Figure 5) that illustrate how different heads allocate focus across temporal features.
weaknesses: Fundamental methodological contradiction regarding GP precomputation and learnability: In Section 3.4 and Appendix C.4, the authors emphasize that GP inference is a 'static, one-time preprocessing cost' that produces negligible trajectory-fitting overhead (Figure 10). However, in Section 3.5, the weighted GP covariance matrix depends on attention weights \(\alpha_{m,k}\) derived from learnable queries \(q_m\) and a learnable 1D CNN \(\Phi_{\text{conv}}\). If \(\alpha_{m,k}\) is learned dynamically during training, the inverse \((K_h + \Sigma_m)^{-1}\) must be recomputed every iteration (precluding one-time precomputation). Conversely, if the paths are precomputed statically before training, the queries and CNN cannot be trained end-to-end with the model. The manuscript never resolves or clarifies this contradiction.

Mathematical errors in the theoretical justification: In Theorem 3.1 and Appendix A.1, the authors argue that for the controlled system \(z'(t) = f_\theta(z(t)) X'(t)\), the \((p+1)\)-th derivative satisfies \(\|d^{p+1}z / dt^{p+1}\| \propto \|d^{p+1}X / dt^{p+1}\|\). By the chain and product rules, higher-order derivatives of \(z(t)\) expand into complex nonlinear combinations of lower-order derivatives, such as \((X')^{p+1}\), cross-products of derivatives of \(X\), and higher derivatives of the vector field \(f_\theta\). Asserting linear proportionality strictly to the \((p+1)\)-th derivative of \(X\) is mathematically incorrect for nonlinear neural vector fields.

Limited and narrow empirical evaluation: The method is evaluated on only three datasets from the UEA archive (CharacterTrajectories, SpokenArabicDigits, UWaveGestureLibrary), all treated with regular grid spacing (\(\Delta t = 1\)). Standard irregularly sampled benchmarks with missing observations (e.g., PhysioNet Challenge 2012, MIMIC-III, or synthetic irregular time series) that originally motivated Neural CDEs are completely omitted.

Poor paper organization and missing core results in the main text: The primary quantitative results table (Table 1), containing all accuracy numbers, wall-clock times, and NFEs, is relegated to Appendix C.1 (page 18). The main text only displays small Pareto scatter plots (Figure 3), making the main manuscript incomplete and self-insufficient without the supplementary material.

Weak justification against discrete baselines: On the evaluated datasets, standard discrete models such as GRU-D achieve competitive accuracy (e.g., 96.57% vs. 98.28% on SpokenArabicDigits) while executing in a fraction of the time (2.02s vs. 7.32s) with zero ODE solver overhead. The practical necessity and advantage of the continuous CDE formulation in this regular-sampling setting remain insufficiently justified.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated approach: The paper clearly identifies numerical stiffness and high derivative magnitude in interpolated control paths as a primary source of high NFE in Neural CDEs, providing a solid theoretical justification (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and 3.4) linking path smoothness directly to solver step sizes.

Effective combination of smoothing and multi-view recovery: Replacing exact interpolants with GP/kernel smoothing reduces solver stiffness, while the multi-head attentive querying (MV-CDE/MVC-CDE) elegantly recovers task-relevant multi-scale temporal features lost during oversmoothing.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across standard classification benchmarks (UEA), irregular sampling/drop rates (Speech Commands, ETTm1 forecasting), high-dimensional settings (963-dim PEMS-SF), and varying solver orders (bosh3, dopri5, dopri8).

Substantial practical gains: The method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy compared to standard CDE baselines while drastically decreasing NFE (up to 5-10x) and wall-clock time, with demonstrated robustness against high noise levels and memory efficiency compared to discrete state-space models like Mamba.
weaknesses: Cubic complexity scaling with sequence length: Computing the GP posterior involves inverting Gram matrices of size N x N (O(N^3) time). While the datasets evaluated feature relatively short sequences (N <= 315), this approach could become a computational bottleneck for very long sequences unless sparse or inducing-point GP approximations are incorporated.

Non-causal / Offline smoothing nature: Full-sequence kernel and GP smoothing inherently look into the future, making them non-causal. While the authors address this via rolling causal windows for ETTm1 forecasting, the paper would benefit from deeper discussion and empirical latency measurements for true real-time streaming applications.

Bandwidth selection and hyperparameter sensitivity: As acknowledged in the limitations, performance and solver efficiency depend heavily on bandwidth tuning. In Table 2, the optimal bandwidth configuration for CharacterTrajectories MVC GP appears homogeneous (BW: [166.6, 166.6, 166.6, 166.6]) despite the emphasis on heterogeneous bandwidths in Appendix C.2, warranting clearer guidelines on hyperparameter selection.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-known practical bottleneck in Neural CDEs: numerical stiffness and excessive function evaluations (high NFE) driven by exact spline interpolation of noisy sequences.

Solid theoretical framework: Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 together with Corollary 3.3 establish a formal connection between path derivative bounds and adaptive solver step-size/NFE scaling, and Theorem 3.4 provides insight into the bottleneck of multi-view integration.

Well-designed architecture: The Multi-View CDE (MV-CDE) and its convolutional extension (MVC-CDE) effectively resolve the primary drawback of smoothing (loss of task-relevant high-frequency details) through attentive multi-scale query extraction and block-diagonal integration.

Thorough and rigorous empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates strong empirical performance across UEA classification benchmarks, irregular sampling on Speech Commands, extreme missingness forecasting on ETTm1, and high-dimensional scaling on the 963-channel PEMS-SF dataset, consistently achieving 4x–14x speedups and notable NFE reductions over standard Neural CDEs while maintaining or improving accuracy.
Comprehensive supplementary analyses, including parameter-matched baselines, memory profiling against Mamba, solver order comparisons, and head diversity regularizations.
weaknesses: Clarity regarding end-to-end backpropagation vs. precomputation: In Section 3.4, GP inference is characterized as a 'static, one-time preprocessing cost'. However, in the weighted GP formulation (Eq. 4), the noise covariance matrix $\Sigma_m$ depends on attention scores $\alpha_{m,k}$, which are functions of learnable parameters ($Q$ and $\Phi_{\text{conv}}$). The manuscript should explicitly clarify how backpropagation through $(K_h + \Sigma_m)^{-1}$ is handled during training and quantify the per-iteration training cost versus one-time precomputations.

Scalability with sequence length: Exact Gaussian Process inference scales as $O(N^3)$ (or $O(M \cdot N^3)$ across heads). While sequence lengths in the evaluated benchmarks are relatively modest ($N \le 315$), this becomes a bottleneck for long-context sequences ($N > 1000$) unless sparse or structured GP approximations are employed.

Offline trajectory assumption: Standard Gaussian Process and Nadaraya-Watson kernel smoothing are fundamentally non-causal operations requiring access to the full sequence (or window). While the authors partially address this with rolling causal windows on ETTm1, the inherent tension between batch smoothing and streaming/online sequential settings warrants deeper discussion relative to causal filtering alternatives (e.g., continuous-discrete Kalman filters).

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Unlike parameter-free deterministic splines, the smoothing framework introduces bandwidths $h_m$ and noise parameters $\sigma^2$, which require dataset-specific sweeps and validation tuning as shown in Table 2.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: The paper tackles a core bottleneck in Neural Controlled Differential Equations (numerical stiffness and excessive NFEs driven by raw, jagged interpolants) from a geometric perspective by regularizing the driving path rather than merely penalizing the latent vector field.

Solid theoretical analysis: Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and 3.4 together with Corollary 3.3 rigorously connect ODE solver local truncation error, path derivatives, kernel bandwidths, and the multi-head integration bottleneck, providing clear theoretical justification for the observed NFE reductions.

Effective multi-view reconstruction design: The proposed multi-head query-based architecture (MV-CDE / MVC-CDE) provides an effective mechanism to counteract the bias/information loss induced by aggressive path smoothing, allowing the network to recover localized temporal patterns.

Comprehensive empirical validation and ablations: The evaluation spans multiple regimes including UEA classification benchmarks, generative forecasting under missingness (ETTm1), irregular sampling robustness (Speech Commands), high spatial dimensions (963-dimensional PEMS-SF), adaptive solver order comparisons (bosh3, dopri5, dopri8), and memory profiling against state-space baselines.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding dynamic vs. static trajectory fitting during training: In Section 3.4 and Appendix C.3/Figure 10, GP trajectory fitting is described as a 'static, one-time preprocessing cost' or 'overhead'. However, in MVC-CDE, the observation noise covariance matrix Sigma_m depends dynamically on attention weights alpha_{m,k}, which are computed from learnable queries and convolutional features. If the queries and front-end CNN are trained end-to-end via backpropagation, the heteroscedastic GP inversion must occur per batch at every training step. The manuscript should explicitly clarify whether full matrix inversion is executed dynamically on every forward pass or if a multi-stage/caching approximation is employed.

Scalability limitations with respect to sequence length N: While the paper benchmarks high feature dimensionality on PEMS-SF (d = 963), the sequence lengths evaluated remain relatively short (N <= 315). Because exact GP regression scales cubically with sequence length O(N^3) and quadratically in memory O(N^2) per head, the approach may become computationally prohibitive on long sequence lengths unless sparse or structured GP approximations are introduced.

Inconsistency between motivation and hyperparameter configurations: The paper argues that heterogeneous bandwidth initialization is essential for capturing multiscale dynamics (e.g., Section C.2 and Figure 8). However, for the main reported results on CharacterTrajectories in Table 2, the best-performing MVC GP model uses identical bandwidths across all heads (BW: [166.6, 166.6, 166.6, 166.6]), which appears to contradict the heterogeneous multiscale premise.

Missing comparisons with recent structured/parallel CDE baselines: Although Structured Linear CDEs (Walker et al., 2025) are cited and discussed conceptually in the related work, they are not included in the empirical benchmark tables alongside Log-NCDE and Mamba.
